stem: In the Kubernetes network model, every Pod gets its own IP address and Pods can reach each other without NAT. Which component actually implements this Pod networking on the nodes?
explanation: Kubernetes defines the network model (unique Pod IPs, Pod-to-Pod reachability without NAT) but leaves the implementation to a Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin. kube-proxy only handles Service virtual IPs, and CoreDNS only handles names.

options.text: kube-proxy, which assigns each Pod its IP address
options.why: kube-proxy programs Service virtual IPs; it does not give Pods their addresses.

options.text: A CNI plugin such as Calico, Cilium or Flannel
options.why: The container runtime calls the CNI plugin to wire up each Pod's network interface and routes.

options.text: CoreDNS, which hands out Pod IPs from its zone
options.why: CoreDNS answers name lookups; it never allocates or routes Pod IPs.

options.text: The API server, which forwards Pod-to-Pod packets
options.why: The API server stores state; data-plane packets never pass through it.

stem: You create a Service without setting `spec.type`. Which kind of Service do you get?
explanation: When `type` is omitted, Kubernetes creates a ClusterIP Service: a stable virtual IP and DNS name that only clients inside the cluster can reach.

options.text: NodePort, reachable on every node
options.why: NodePort must be requested explicitly with `type: NodePort`.

options.text: LoadBalancer, if the cluster runs in a cloud
options.why: A cloud load balancer is only provisioned for `type: LoadBalancer`.

options.text: ClusterIP, internal to the cluster
options.why: ClusterIP is the default type and gives an internal virtual IP.

options.text: Headless, with no virtual IP at all
options.why: Headless requires `clusterIP: None` to be set on purpose.

stem: Creating an Ingress resource in a fresh cluster is enough, on its own, to start routing external HTTP traffic to your Services.
explanation: Kubernetes ships no Ingress controller by default. You must deploy one (or use a managed one) and point Ingresses at it with `ingressClassName`; otherwise the Ingress object just sits there.

options.text: True
options.why: An Ingress is only configuration; something must read it and act on it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: without an Ingress controller running in the cluster, an Ingress resource has no effect.

stem: What is the default port range that Kubernetes allocates NodePort Services from? Type it as two numbers separated by a hyphen.
explanation: By default the API server allocates NodePorts from 30000–32767. Administrators can change it with the `--service-node-port-range` flag.

stem: Match each Service type with what it does.
explanation: The types build on one another: NodePort adds a node port to a ClusterIP, and LoadBalancer adds an external load balancer in front of the node ports. ExternalName is different: it is only a DNS alias.

options.text: Gives a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster
Opens the same port on every node in addition to a cluster IP
Asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer
Returns a DNS CNAME to an outside hostname, with no proxying

stem: A Service named `api` lives in the `payments` namespace of a cluster using the default `cluster.local` domain. What is its fully qualified DNS name?
explanation: Cluster DNS gives every Service an A/AAAA record at `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`, here `api.payments.svc.cluster.local`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: DNS for Services and Pods

options.text: `payments.api.svc.cluster.local`
options.why: The Service name comes first, then the namespace.

options.text: `api.payments.svc.cluster.local`
options.why: Service DNS names follow `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`.

options.text: `api.payments.svc.default.cluster.local`
options.why: There is no extra `default` label; the namespace already follows the Service name.

options.text: `api.cluster.local`
options.why: That drops the namespace, so it cannot identify the Service.

stem: Which two conditions decide whether a Pod receives traffic sent to a Service's ClusterIP? (Choose two.)
explanation: The endpoint controller builds EndpointSlices from Pods whose labels match the selector, and marks only Ready Pods as ready. kube-proxy forwards Service traffic to the ready endpoints.

options.text: The Pod's labels match the Service's `selector`
options.why: The selector determines which Pods are candidate endpoints.

options.text: The Pod is Ready, for example its readiness probe passes
options.why: Only Ready Pods are marked ready in the EndpointSlices that kube-proxy uses.

options.text: The Pod runs on the same node as the client
options.why: Service routing is cluster-wide by default; locality is optional.

options.text: The Pod's container declares the port with `containerPort`
options.why: `containerPort` is informational; traffic reaches any port the process listens on.

options.text: The Pod has the same name as the Service
options.why: Names are irrelevant; selection is purely by labels.

stem: A developer runs `kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80` to test the API. What is this command meant for?
explanation: `kubectl port-forward` opens a local port that tunnels through the API server to one Pod. It is a debugging tool, not a way to expose or load-balance a Service.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Use Port Forwarding to Access Applications in a Cluster

options.text: Temporary access from their own machine for debugging
options.why: It tunnels through the API server to a Pod behind the Service, only for the local user.

options.text: Exposing the Service to the internet for customers
options.why: The tunnel lives on one laptop and ends when the command stops.

options.text: Changing the Service's port from 80 to 8080 permanently
options.why: It changes nothing on the Service; it only opens a local listener.

options.text: Load balancing requests across every Pod of the Service
options.why: port-forward picks a single Pod and sends all traffic to it.

stem:
The Service below has no endpoints, and requests to it time out. Why?

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
# Pod template labels from the Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: frontend
    tier: web
```
explanation: A Service selects Pods whose labels include every key/value pair in its selector. No Pod has `app=web`, so the EndpointSlices are empty. Fix the selector (`app: frontend`) or the Pod labels.

options.text: `targetPort` must equal `port` for endpoints to be created
options.why: Different `port` and `targetPort` values are normal and allowed.

options.text: Selector `app: web` matches no Pod (they are `app: frontend`)
options.why: Selectors match label keys and values, so `tier: web` does not count.

options.text: Services need a `containerPort: 8080` entry declared in the Pod spec
options.why: `containerPort` is informational and doesn't affect endpoint creation.

options.text: A Service must have the same name as the Deployment
options.why: Names play no part in selecting Pods.

stem: A Service has `port: 80` and `targetPort: 8080`. The container actually listens on port 3000. What happens when another Pod calls `http://web/`?
explanation: kube-proxy rewrites traffic for the Service port (80) to the Pod IP and `targetPort` (8080). Because the process listens on 3000, the client gets connection refused even though the Service has endpoints. Set `targetPort: 3000` or use a named port.

options.text: kube-proxy notices the mismatch and forwards to port 3000
options.why: kube-proxy never inspects which ports a container listens on.

options.text: The request reaches the app because Services map to the first open port
options.why: Traffic goes exactly to `targetPort`; there is no port discovery.

options.text: Traffic is sent to port 8080 on the Pod and is refused
options.why: Nothing listens on 8080, so the connection is reset.

options.text: The Service fails validation and is never created
options.why: The API server cannot know what the process will listen on.

stem: A Service is defined with `clusterIP: None` and a selector. What does a DNS lookup of its name return?
explanation: A headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) has no virtual IP and is not proxied. DNS returns the IPs of the ready Pods it selects, which lets clients do their own load balancing or address individual Pods.

options.text: Nothing, because a Service without a cluster IP has no DNS record
options.why: Headless Services do get DNS records; they just aren't a virtual IP.

options.text: A single virtual IP that kube-proxy balances behind the scenes
options.why: Headless means kube-proxy doesn't handle it and there is no virtual IP.

options.text: One A/AAAA record per ready Pod, with the Pods' own IPs
options.why: Clients get the Pod IPs directly and choose among them.

options.text: A CNAME pointing at an external hostname
options.why: That describes an ExternalName Service, not a headless one.

stem: A Pod in the `shop` namespace needs to call the Service `api` in the `payments` namespace (cluster domain `cluster.local`). Which two hostnames resolve correctly? (Choose two.)
explanation: A Pod's resolv.conf searches `<own-ns>.svc.cluster.local`, `svc.cluster.local` and `cluster.local`. `api.payments` becomes `api.payments.svc.cluster.local`, while bare `api` only looks in the caller's own namespace.
reference: Kubernetes docs: DNS for Services and Pods

options.text: `api.payments`
options.why: The search path appends `svc.cluster.local`, completing the name.

options.text: `api.payments.svc.cluster.local`
options.why: The fully qualified name always works.

options.text: `api`
options.why: A bare name is completed with the caller's own namespace, giving `api.shop`.

options.text: `payments.api`
options.why: The namespace goes after the Service name, not before it.

options.text: `api.svc.cluster.local`
options.why: This leaves out the namespace, which is required.

stem: An external client sends a request to `node-a:31080`, the NodePort of a Service whose Pods listen on `targetPort: 8080`. Put the hops in order.
explanation: NodePort traffic hits any node, where kube-proxy's iptables/nftables rules pick an endpoint (possibly on another node) and rewrite the destination to the Pod IP and target port. The Pod then handles the request.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: The packet arrives at node-a on port 31080
kube-proxy's rules on node-a match the NodePort and choose a ready endpoint
The packet is DNATed to the chosen Pod IP and port 8080
The container process receives the request on port 8080

stem: An ExternalName Service (`externalName: db.example.com`) makes kube-proxy forward Pod traffic to `db.example.com`.
explanation: ExternalName Services exist only in DNS. Looking up the Service name returns a CNAME record; kube-proxy never sees the traffic, and ports in the Service spec are not used for forwarding.

options.text: True
options.why: ExternalName involves no proxying at all.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: cluster DNS just returns a CNAME to `db.example.com`, and the client connects there directly.

stem: A Service uses `targetPort: http`. Pods from the old version declare `containerPort: 8080` named `http`, and Pods from the new version declare `containerPort: 9090` named `http`. During the rollout, what happens?
explanation: A named `targetPort` is resolved against each Pod's `ports[].name`, so the EndpointSlices can carry different port numbers for the same name. That lets you change the container port without touching the Service.

options.text: Each Pod receives traffic on its own port named `http`
options.why: Named target ports are resolved per Pod, so both versions work side by side.

options.text: All traffic goes to 8080 because the first Pod sets the port
options.why: The name is looked up separately for every endpoint.

options.text: The Service rejects the mixed ports until the rollout ends
options.why: Mixed port numbers for one name are a supported pattern.

options.text: Requests fail because `targetPort` must be numeric
options.why: `targetPort` can be a number or a port name.

stem: An Ingress rule uses `path: /api` with `pathType: Prefix`. Which request path does it NOT match?
explanation: With `pathType: Prefix`, Kubernetes splits the path on `/` and matches element by element. `/api` matches `/api`, `/api/` and `/api/v1/orders`, but not `/apiv2`, which is a different element.

options.text: `/api`
options.why: The exact path is a prefix of itself, so it matches.

options.text: `/api/v1/orders`
options.why: `/api` matches element by element: the first path element is `api`.

options.text: `/apiv2`
options.why: Prefix matching compares whole path elements, and `apiv2` is not `api`.

options.text: `/api/`
options.why: The trailing slash still leaves `api` as the first element.

stem: A cluster runs two Ingress controllers. Which field in the Ingress `spec` selects the controller that should handle it? Type the field name.
explanation: `spec.ingressClassName` names an IngressClass, which points to a specific controller. It replaces the deprecated `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation.

stem: A Service runs in a cluster spread across three zones. To cut cross-zone traffic costs you set `spec.trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone`. What does this field do?

options.text: It guarantees traffic never leaves the client's zone, failing requests if none are local
options.why: It is a preference: implementations can still send traffic to other zones when needed.

options.text: It expresses a preference for routing to endpoints in the same zone as the client
options.why: Traffic distribution states routing preferences rather than strict guarantees.

options.text: It replaces `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and preserves the client's source IP
options.why: Source IP preservation is a traffic-policy feature; trafficDistribution only influences endpoint choice.

options.text: It moves the Service's endpoints to new Pods scheduled in the client's zone
options.why: It doesn't schedule or move Pods; it only affects which existing endpoints receive traffic.

explanation: The Service `trafficDistribution` field lets you express routing preferences, such as sending traffic to topologically closer endpoints, to optimise for performance, cost or reliability. Unlike traffic policies, which have strict semantic guarantees, it is a preference. Supported values include `PreferSameZone` and `PreferSameNode`; `PreferClose` is the older, deprecated alias for `PreferSameZone`. If the field is unset, the implementation applies its default routing.

stem: Match each Gateway API resource with the role that typically owns it.
explanation: Gateway API splits Ingress's single object into role-oriented resources: providers define GatewayClasses, operators deploy Gateways (listeners, TLS), developers attach HTTPRoutes, and a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace allows cross-namespace references.

options.text: Infrastructure provider
Cluster operator
Application developer

stem: A gRPC client talks to a ClusterIP Service backed by 5 Pods. Monitoring shows one Pod handles almost all requests. Why?
explanation: kube-proxy works at layer 4: it chooses an endpoint per connection, not per request. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection, so a single client pins to one Pod. Fixes include client-side balancing over a headless Service, or an L7 proxy or service mesh that balances per request.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: kube-proxy uses source-IP hashing, so each client always maps to one Pod
options.why: The default iptables mode picks endpoints randomly per new connection.

options.text: gRPC reuses one HTTP/2 connection, and kube-proxy balances per connection
options.why: Once the connection is set up, all its requests go to the same Pod.

options.text: Four of the Pods failed their readiness probes
options.why: That is possible, but would show up as missing endpoints rather than a gRPC pattern.

options.text: ClusterIP Services only use the first endpoint unless `sessionAffinity` is set
options.why: ClusterIP spreads new connections; affinity only makes them stickier.

stem: A LoadBalancer Service uses the default `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`. The application logs show node IPs instead of real client IPs. Why?
explanation: With `Cluster`, any node accepts traffic and may forward it to a Pod elsewhere. To make replies come back through the same node, it source-NATs the packet, so the Pod sees a node IP. `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` keeps traffic on nodes with local endpoints and preserves the client IP.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: The cloud load balancer always strips the client IP
options.why: With `Local`, the same load balancer preserves it.

options.text: Nodes SNAT traffic they forward to Pods on other nodes
options.why: SNAT keeps the return path correct but replaces the source IP.

options.text: kube-proxy rewrites the source IP to block spoofing
options.why: There is no anti-spoofing rewrite; the SNAT exists for routing.

options.text: Pods only see client IPs when they use `hostNetwork: true`
options.why: Pod networking can show client IPs with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`.

stem: You switch a LoadBalancer Service to `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`. Which two consequences should you expect? (Choose two.)
explanation: `Local` routes external traffic only to Pods on the receiving node, so the client IP is preserved. Nodes without ready local endpoints fail the `healthCheckNodePort` probe and are taken out of rotation. The load balancer splits by node, so uneven Pod placement causes uneven load.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: Pods see the original client source IP
options.why: Traffic is no longer SNATed to another node.

options.text: Load can become uneven, because the load balancer spreads by node, not by Pod
options.why: A node with one Pod and a node with three get similar shares.

options.text: Nodes without a local Pod forward traffic to other nodes
options.why: With `Local`, they drop it and fail the health check instead.

options.text: The Service loses its ClusterIP for in-cluster clients
options.why: In-cluster traffic to the ClusterIP is unaffected.

options.text: The cloud load balancer is removed and replaced by NodePorts
options.why: The external load balancer stays in place.

stem: A Pod calls `api.example.com` thousands of times per minute, and DNS latency is high. Its `/etc/resolv.conf` has `search shop.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local` and `options ndots:5`. What is happening?
explanation: A name with fewer dots than `ndots` (5) is first tried with each search suffix, such as `api.example.com.shop.svc.cluster.local`, and each attempt returns NXDOMAIN before the absolute name is tried. Use a trailing dot (`api.example.com.`) or lower `ndots` in `dnsConfig` for heavy external lookups.
reference: Kubernetes docs: DNS for Services and Pods

options.text: CoreDNS refuses to resolve names that are outside the cluster domain
options.why: CoreDNS forwards external names upstream normally.

options.text: Each search domain is tried first, as the name has under 5 dots
options.why: Each lookup causes several failed queries first.

options.text: The `search` list is ignored for names that contain dots
options.why: Names with fewer than `ndots` dots still use the search list first.

options.text: `ndots:5` makes every query repeat 5 times for reliability
options.why: `ndots` is a threshold for search-list use, not a retry count.

stem: A Pod's readiness probe starts failing while its liveness probe keeps passing. Which two statements describe what happens? (Choose two.)
explanation: Readiness controls whether a Pod is marked ready in EndpointSlices. When it fails, kube-proxy stops sending new Service traffic there, but the container keeps running. Liveness failures are what cause the kubelet to restart a container.

options.text: The Pod is marked not ready in the Service's EndpointSlices and stops getting new Service traffic
options.why: Readiness gates traffic, not the container's life.

options.text: The container keeps running and is not restarted
options.why: Only failing liveness probes trigger restarts.

options.text: The kubelet restarts the container to recover readiness
options.why: Readiness failures never cause a restart.

options.text: The Deployment deletes the Pod and creates a replacement
options.why: Controllers don't replace Pods for being unready.

options.text: The Service is deleted until a Pod becomes ready again
options.why: The Service object is never removed by probe results.

stem: A StatefulSet `db` with `serviceName: db` runs 3 replicas in namespace `data`. What must be true for `db-0.db.data.svc.cluster.local` to resolve to the first replica?
explanation: A StatefulSet's `serviceName` must name a headless Service. That Service creates `<pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.<domain>` records for each Pod, giving stable network identities such as `db-0.db.data.svc.cluster.local`.

options.why: Per-Pod DNS records come from the governing headless Service.

options.why: Pod DNS records work with normal Pod networking.

options.why: StatefulSets don't need a Service per Pod.

stem: A ClusterIP Service behind an Ingress controller uses `sessionAffinity: ClientIP`. Users still lose their in-memory sessions. Why?
explanation: The Ingress controller opens its own connections to the Service, so ClientIP affinity groups traffic by controller Pod, not by user. For per-user stickiness, configure cookie-based affinity in the Ingress controller, or store sessions outside the Pods.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.why: The default stickiness timeout is 10800 seconds (3 hours).

options.why: It applies to ClusterIP traffic handled by kube-proxy.

options.why: Affinity is keyed on the source IP of the connection that reaches the Service.

options.text: Affinity requires a headless Service to work
options.why: Headless Services aren't proxied, so affinity doesn't apply to them at all.

stem: If `ping` to a Service's ClusterIP gets no reply from inside a Pod, that proves the Service is broken.
explanation: Kubernetes docs note that Service IPs are not answered by a single host; kube-proxy only matches the protocols and ports defined on the Service. ICMP usually goes unanswered. Test with the real protocol, for example `curl` or `nc` to the Service port.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: True

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Service IPs aren't answered by any single host, so ICMP often fails even when TCP works.

stem: A Pod in namespace `shop` (cluster domain `cluster.local`, `ndots:5`) looks up the short name `api`. Put the names its resolver tries in order.
explanation: The search list is `<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, then `svc.cluster.local`, then `cluster.local`. Because `api` has fewer dots than `ndots`, each suffix is tried before the name on its own. The first one matches when `api` exists in the Pod's own namespace.

explanation: A LoadBalancer Service is a NodePort Service (which is a ClusterIP Service) plus an external load balancer that the cloud controller manager provisions. Public DNS and Ingress are separate concerns.

stem: A node-local cache Service sets `internalTrafficPolicy: Local`. A client Pod runs on a node with no cache Pod. What happens to its requests to the Service?
explanation: `internalTrafficPolicy: Local` tells kube-proxy to use only endpoints on the client's node. If there are none, kube-proxy drops the traffic. That is why it suits Services backed by a DaemonSet that runs on every node.

explanation: The Ingress `tls` section names a Secret in the Ingress's namespace that contains `tls.crt` and `tls.key`. The controller presents that certificate for the listed hosts and terminates TLS before proxying to the Services.

stem: A headless Service backs a StatefulSet whose Pods must find each other through DNS before they are Ready. Which Service spec field makes DNS publish not-ready Pods too? Type the field name.
explanation: Setting `spec.publishNotReadyAddresses: true` includes Pods regardless of readiness in the Service's DNS records. Clustered databases use it so peers can discover each other while bootstrapping.

stem: During every rolling update, clients behind an Ingress see a burst of 502 errors from Pods that are shutting down. The app exits as soon as it gets SIGTERM. What is the most effective fix?
explanation: When a Pod is deleted, the endpoint update and the kubelet's shutdown run concurrently. kube-proxy and Ingress controllers may still send requests for a few seconds. A `preStop` hook such as `sleep 5`, or handling SIGTERM by draining before exit, lets in-flight routing catch up.

options.why: A longer grace period changes nothing if the app exits on SIGTERM at once.

options.why: Old Pods still terminate once new ones are ready.

options.why: That makes routing worse, not better.

options.text: 33%, because node A is one of three healthy targets
options.why: Only two nodes are targets, not three.

options.text: 50%: all of node A's half goes to its single Pod
options.why: Each node keeps its traffic local, so node A's Pod gets that node's whole share.

options.text: 0%, because nodes with fewer Pods are taken out of rotation
options.why: A node is removed only when it has zero ready local Pods.

stem: A firewall only allows clients to reach node C on a NodePort Service. Node C runs none of the Service's Pods. Which statement is correct?
explanation: With `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`, any node accepts the NodePort traffic and forwards it, SNATed, to a ready Pod anywhere. With `Local`, a node with no local ready endpoints drops the traffic, so clients that can only reach node C time out.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

options.text: It fails under both policies, since node C has no Pods
options.why: With `Cluster`, node C forwards to Pods on other nodes.

options.text: It works with `Cluster` but times out with `Local`
options.why: Only `Cluster` forwards to endpoints on other nodes.

options.text: It works under both policies with no difference
options.why: `Local` keeps traffic on nodes that have local endpoints.

options.text: It works with `Local` but fails with `Cluster`
options.why: The behaviour is the other way round.

stem: Ingress NGINX, the Kubernetes community controller, stopped receiving releases, bug fixes and security fixes after March 2026, although existing installations keep working.
explanation: Kubernetes SIG Network and the Security Response Committee announced in November 2025 that Ingress NGINX would be retired. Best-effort maintenance ran until March 2026; after that there are no releases or security fixes. Existing deployments keep working, and the project recommends migrating to Gateway API or another controller.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: Kubernetes SIG Network retired Ingress NGINX in March 2026, after best-effort maintenance ended.

options.text: False
options.why: The retirement was announced in November 2025 and took effect in March 2026.

stem: You create a Service with no selector, to front an external database at 10.20.0.5:5432, and add an EndpointSlice by hand. Traffic to the Service still goes nowhere. What is the most likely mistake?
explanation: For a Service without a selector, you create EndpointSlices yourself. They must carry the label `kubernetes.io/service-name: <service-name>` (and should set `endpointslice.kubernetes.io/managed-by` to your own value). Without that label, nothing ties the slice to the Service.

options.text: Selector-less Services can't be given endpoints of any kind
options.why: Selector-less Services exist exactly so you can supply endpoints yourself.

options.text: The EndpointSlice must be in `kube-system`
options.why: It must be in the same namespace as the Service.

options.text: The slice lacks the `kubernetes.io/service-name` label
options.why: kube-proxy links slices to a Service through that label.

options.text: External IPs are forbidden in EndpointSlices
options.why: IPs outside the cluster are allowed in manual endpoints.

stem: Which two statements about service meshes are accurate? (Choose two.)
explanation: Meshes add L7 traffic management, such as per-request balancing, retries and mTLS, on top of the CNI network. Sidecar meshes inject a proxy into each Pod; Istio's ambient mode uses per-node ztunnel proxies for L4 and optional waypoint proxies for L7. Retries need care with non-idempotent operations.

options.text: An L7 proxy balances per request, which fixes gRPC requests pinning to one Pod
options.why: The proxy spreads requests within long-lived HTTP/2 connections.

options.text: Ambient mode (Istio) handles L4 traffic with node-level proxies instead of a per-Pod sidecar
options.why: ztunnel runs per node, and waypoint proxies add L7 when needed.

options.text: A mesh replaces the CNI plugin and assigns Pod IPs
options.why: Meshes run on top of the Pod network that the CNI provides.

options.text: Mesh retries are safe for every request, including non-idempotent POSTs
options.why: Retrying non-idempotent calls can duplicate side effects.

options.text: Mutual TLS in a mesh needs no certificates
options.why: The mesh issues and rotates workload certificates for you.

stem: In a cluster configured for IPv4 only, you apply a Service with `ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack`. What happens?
explanation: `ipFamilyPolicy` can be `SingleStack`, `PreferDualStack` or `RequireDualStack`. `PreferDualStack` uses both families when they exist and falls back otherwise; `RequireDualStack` fails unless the cluster has both IPv4 and IPv6 Service ranges.

options.text: It is created with only an IPv4 cluster IP
options.why: That describes `PreferDualStack`, which falls back silently.

options.text: The API server rejects it: both IP families are required
options.why: `RequireDualStack` insists on both families.

options.text: It is created with an IPv6 address borrowed from the node network
options.why: Service IPs only come from configured Service CIDRs.

options.text: It is created with no cluster IP, like a headless Service
options.why: Headless needs `clusterIP: None`, not an IP family policy.

stem: After a default-deny egress NetworkPolicy is applied to namespace `shop`, Pods there can no longer reach `api.payments` by name, yet connecting to its ClusterIP directly also fails. An egress rule to the `payments` Pods on TCP 8080 was added. What else is needed?
explanation: Default-deny egress blocks DNS too, so name resolution fails first. The ClusterIP attempt also fails if the allow rule doesn't match the destination port the Pod actually listens on. NetworkPolicies are evaluated against Pod IPs and target ports, after Service translation. Add an egress rule to the kube-dns/CoreDNS Pods on port 53.

options.text: An egress rule allowing port 53 to the cluster DNS Pods
options.why: Without DNS egress, name lookups fail before any connection starts.

options.text: An ingress rule on the CoreDNS Pods allowing all namespaces
options.why: The block is on the client's egress, not on CoreDNS's ingress.

options.text: A rule allowing egress to the Service's ClusterIP on port 80
options.why: Policies match the Pod IPs and ports after kube-proxy's rewrite.

options.text: Nothing: NetworkPolicy never applies to DNS traffic
options.why: DNS is ordinary UDP/TCP traffic and is filtered like any other.

stem: On a bare-metal cluster with no cloud provider integration, a Service of `type: LoadBalancer` shows `EXTERNAL-IP <pending>` indefinitely. Why?
explanation: Kubernetes records the request for a load balancer, but an implementation, such as a cloud controller manager or MetalLB on bare metal, must assign an address. Without one, the status stays pending. The ClusterIP and NodePort parts still work.

options.text: LoadBalancer Services take up to an hour to provision
options.why: Waiting won't help; nothing is provisioning the load balancer.

options.text: The Service needs `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` first
options.why: The traffic policy doesn't control provisioning.

options.text: Nothing implements LoadBalancer here, such as MetalLB
options.why: Kubernetes only requests a load balancer; a controller must provide it.

options.text: Bare-metal nodes can't run NodePorts, which LoadBalancer requires
options.why: NodePorts work on any cluster.

stem: Match each symptom with its most likely cause.
explanation: Each symptom points to one layer: no endpoints means selection or readiness; refused connections mean the wrong port; NXDOMAIN on a short name means the wrong namespace; node IPs in the logs mean the traffic was SNATed.

options.text: The Service selector doesn't match any Pod labels
`targetPort` points to a port the process isn't listening on
A bare service name is resolved from a different namespace
`externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` SNATs forwarded traffic

prompts.text: `kubectl get endpointslices` shows no endpoints for the Service
Endpoints exist, but connections are refused
`nslookup orders` returns NXDOMAIN from a Pod in another namespace
Access logs show node IPs instead of client IPs

stem: A Pod with a `preStop` hook is deleted while it serves traffic. Put the kubelet's shutdown steps in order.
explanation: Deletion marks the Pod Terminating and starts the grace period; at the same time, endpoint controllers stop routing to it. The kubelet runs `preStop`, then sends SIGTERM, and finally SIGKILL if the grace period expires. The grace period covers both the hook and the shutdown.

options.text: The API server sets the Pod's deletion timestamp and it shows as Terminating
The kubelet runs the container's `preStop` hook
The kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container's main process
If the container is still running when the grace period ends, the kubelet sends SIGKILL
